source.title: Global Dynamics of Heavy-Tailed SGDs in Nonconvex Loss Landscape: Characterization and Control

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some equations and table formatting are flattened, but the reported experiment values can be assigned to their methods and tasks.
record.tranche_reason: The study runs its own deep-learning experiments comparing a new heavy-tail injection and clipping training method with SGD and Adam baselines, and reports test accuracy and expected sharpness. These results bear on generalization, but do not test a listed claim version directly.
record.gate_note: The paper’s theoretical and simulation results about avoiding wide or narrow minima are not rows for the listed versions. The deep-learning tables report the study’s own training-method comparisons; the proposed method’s results are retained, as are its SGD and Adam comparators. The paper does not measure training-to-test error gaps or magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.test_reason: The study uses the flat-minima generalization hypothesis to develop and evaluate a training method. None of V1–V8 is directly tested: notably, the large- and small-batch baselines use equal iteration counts, not equal epoch budgets, and expected sharpness is neither magnitude-aware nor compared with training-to-test gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors conclude that injecting and clipping heavy-tailed updates favors flatter solutions and improves test performance over their SGD and tuned Adam baselines. Their reported accuracy improvements are consistent across configurations, whereas expected sharpness is not uniformly lower for every proposed-method configuration.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes injecting Pareto-scaled heavy-tailed noise and clipping gradients, then compares that training procedure with SGD and Adam baselines; it does not reproduce the listed versions’ methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary across dataset, architecture, training method, and whether heavy-tailed noise is clipped. The Adam experiment also uses CIFAR10 versus CIFAR100 and three WRN configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal iteration counts, LB and SB accuracies are 68.77% versus 68.91% on corrupted FashionMNIST, 82.91% versus 85.89% on SVHN, and 69.78% versus 74.53% on CIFAR10. LB processes 12 or 10 times as many examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under these fixed-iteration recipes, smaller batches yield higher mean test accuracy, with little difference on corrupted FashionMNIST; this does not establish a fixed-epoch batch penalty.

fits_no_version.finding: Both proposed injection-and-clipping methods exceed the SGD comparators' mean test accuracies on all three ablation tasks. Unclipped noise performs poorly despite a smaller learning rate, longer training, and weight clipping.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested heavy-tail injection-and-clipping recipes improve test accuracy relative to these SGD baselines; removing gradient clipping produces unstable, poorer performance under the separately adjusted recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding truncated heavy-tailed updates to Adam improves mean accuracy in all six WRN configurations, by 1.10–1.58 percentage points on CIFAR10 and 2.05–2.85 points on CIFAR100.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Additional truncated heavy-tailed updates improve accuracy over the tuned Adam baselines in these WRN experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: The ablation reports expected absolute training-loss changes under isotropic Gaussian weight perturbations. The proposed recipes often reduce this measure, but CIFAR10 method 2 has higher expected sharpness than SB despite higher accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: These recipes often improve accuracy and reduce unscaled expected sharpness, without establishing V7's magnitude-aware sharpness–generalization-gap relationship.

record.problems: The deep-learning results are on FashionMNIST, SVHN, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 only. Each reported interval is estimated over 5 runs; the unclipped-noise method has very large reported ranges. Expected sharpness is not the magnitude-aware measure in V7 and is not paired with a measured training-to-test error gap.
record.rows_left_out: None of the reported deep-learning table values were left out. The theory and R1 simulation are not extracted as rows because they do not measure a listed version’s claimed generalization behavior.

untested.parts: No comparison of near-perfect random-label fitting with natural-label generalization and chance-level random-label test accuracy. Corrupting 200 of 1200 FashionMNIST labels does not establish this.
No controlled width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold; the WRNs also differ in depth.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
No matched adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison under the specified tuning conditions.
No batch-size comparison at fixed epoch budgets, workload-dependent threshold sweep, or controlled test of remedies for a fixed-epoch large-batch penalty.
No magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, measured training-to-test gaps, similarly low training-loss check, or ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
No influence-based identification and removal of memorized examples followed by retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The numerical values in the extracted rows match the supplied tables. Proposed-method and ablation performance rows belong under fits_no_version rather than evidence for V1–V8. Contrary to rows_left_out, Table 4.4's twelve expected-sharpness values were omitted; these still do not bear on V7, so they are not listed in missing. In particular, CIFAR100 WRN28-10 has higher mean expected sharpness with the proposed method (0.00036 versus 0.00032), despite better test accuracy.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare fitting fixed random labels with generalization on natural labels.
No network-width sweep around the zero-training-error threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
Does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD under the version’s tuning conditions; Adam is compared with Adam plus the proposed method.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
Reports expected sharpness, but does not test magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its relationship with the training-to-test gap.
